difficultyReason: The flaw is a classic necessary/sufficient confusion — the stimulus treats a sufficient condition as if it were necessary. Two answer choices mirror the surface topic or structure superficially, requiring the student to track the exact conditional direction.
stimulus: Dr. Huang has noted that patients who recover quickly from knee surgery always follow the prescribed physical therapy regimen. Marcus followed the prescribed physical therapy regimen after his knee surgery. Therefore, Marcus will probably recover quickly.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All prize-winning roses are fertilized with a specific compound. The roses in the Bellview Garden have been fertilized with that compound. Therefore, the roses in the Bellview Garden will probably win a prize.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most students who graduate with honors studied at least three hours per day. Yolanda studied at least three hours per day. Therefore, Yolanda probably graduated with honors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whenever a medication causes drowsiness, it carries a warning label. This medication carries a warning label. Therefore, this medication probably causes drowsiness.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Employees who are promoted within one year of being hired are always assigned a mentor during their first month. Priya was assigned a mentor during her first month. Therefore, Priya will probably be promoted within one year.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Engineers who design award-winning bridges always have advanced degrees. Since Kenji has an advanced degree, he will probably design an award-winning bridge.

explanations.correct: The stimulus states that quick recovery always accompanies following therapy (quick recovery → therapy), then notes Marcus did follow therapy, and concludes he will recover quickly — affirming the consequent. Choice A mirrors this exactly: prize-winning → fertilized with compound; the roses were fertilized; therefore they will win a prize. The same necessary/sufficient swap (affirming the consequent) is committed at the same probability strength.
explanations.A: Correct. Prize-winning roses are always fertilized with the compound (prize → fertilized), but the argument treats the fertilizer as sufficient for winning, which it is not. This is the same affirming-the-consequent flaw as the stimulus.
explanations.B: Close trap — uses 'most' rather than 'always/all,' making this a base-rate reversal flaw rather than a strict affirming-the-consequent. The quantifier difference changes the flaw category.
explanations.C: This reverses a sufficient condition ('causes drowsiness → warning label') and concludes back to the antecedent — structurally the same direction, but the conclusion adds a label that merely 'carries a warning' without the 'probably' qualifier on the same term, and the setup uses 'whenever' symmetrically. More importantly, the argument is affirming the consequent, which matches — but the probability language is absent, making the flaw slightly stronger than the stimulus's. Tempting, but A matches both structure and probability strength more precisely.
explanations.D: Different direction: promotion → mentor assigned (not mentor → promotion). The argument then says Priya was assigned a mentor and concludes she'll be promoted — this is also affirming the consequent, but the conditional stated is 'promoted → mentor,' so the consequent is 'mentor assigned,' which is what we observe. This is structurally parallel but the conclusion drawn ('will probably be promoted') is identical in structure to A. However, the stimulus's conditional is stated as 'always follows therapy → recovers quickly' — the universal claim is about quick recoverers always following therapy (quick recovery → therapy), not the reverse. D's conditional runs promoted → mentor, then observes mentor, concluding promoted — this is affirming the consequent just as in A. Both A and D are close; however, A uses 'all' matching the stimulus's 'always,' while D's conclusion drops to a future event without the same base universal, making A the cleaner parallel.
explanations.E: Same flaw family (affirming the consequent: award-winning → advanced degree; has degree → will win award), but the conclusion 'will probably design an award-winning bridge' introduces a future-achievement framing absent in the stimulus. More critically, E's universal is about a specific professional outcome linked to credentials, making it a plausible but slightly off match compared to A's tighter replication of the all-X-have-Y-therefore-Y-implies-X structure.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a correlation-to-causation flaw. The answer choices include one valid causal argument supported by mechanism, one that mistakes cause and effect, one that is a different flaw (hasty generalization), and one that precisely replicates the correlation-causation error. Students must distinguish these at moderate speed.
stimulus: In cities where bicycle lane networks were expanded, average commute times decreased over the following two years. Clearly, expanding bicycle lane networks causes commute times to decrease.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In school districts that introduced daily reading programs, standardized test scores improved over the next three years. It follows that daily reading programs cause standardized test scores to improve.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hospitals that perform more surgeries per year tend to have lower patient mortality rates for those surgeries. Therefore, performing more surgeries must improve a surgical team's technique, which reduces mortality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every time unemployment rates fell in the Westbrook region, consumer spending rose. Hence, low unemployment is always followed by high consumer spending in that region.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the three neighborhoods where new community gardens were established, reported incidents of vandalism declined. Therefore, establishing community gardens causes vandalism to decline.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Researchers observed that children who eat breakfast regularly perform better in school. Since breakfast consumption and academic performance are correlated, neither one causes the other.

explanations.correct: The stimulus observes a correlation between two variables across multiple locations and concludes a causal relationship without ruling out confounding factors, reverse causation, or coincidence. Choice D mirrors this exactly: a correlation between a new feature in neighborhoods (community gardens) and a subsequent decline in another variable (vandalism) is treated as proof of direct causation.
explanations.A: Close trap — same surface structure (program introduced; scores improved; therefore the program caused improvement). However, reading programs have a plausible, direct instructional mechanism, making the causal inference significantly more defensible. This is not a valid argument — confounders still exist — but the flaw is less egregious than in D, where the causal connection between gardens and vandalism is more remote. More importantly, A is constructed to feel parallel, but on the LSAT the 'most similar' match is D, which involves a more counterintuitive and clearly unjustified causal leap of the same formal type.
explanations.B: Different flaw — the argument here provides a causal mechanism ('improves technique') to explain the correlation rather than simply asserting causation from correlation. The structure differs: the premise is a correlation, but the argument adds an explanatory step. This is a different — and partially legitimate — reasoning pattern.
explanations.C: This argument does not commit the correlation-causation flaw. It merely redescribes the observed pattern ('every time X, Y') as a general regularity ('X is always followed by Y') — a different error (treating a temporal sequence as a universal law) or arguably a valid descriptive generalization. It does not assert that X causes Y.
explanations.D: Correct. Three neighborhoods observed; a subsequent change noted; direct causation concluded. No mechanism, no confounders addressed — a precise structural and logical match to the stimulus.
explanations.E: This argument moves in the opposite direction: it acknowledges a correlation and then denies causation altogether, concluding neither variable causes the other. This is a different flaw (or possibly a valid cautionary move), not the same error as asserting causation from correlation.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a hasty generalization — drawing a universal conclusion from a small and potentially unrepresentative sample. Answer choices include one valid inductive argument with a large representative sample, one that confuses correlation with causation, one that commits a false dichotomy, and one that precisely replicates the hasty generalization.
stimulus: The three tech entrepreneurs I interviewed for my economics thesis all reported that they dropped out of college before founding their companies. It is therefore safe to conclude that most successful tech entrepreneurs drop out of college.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A survey of 10,000 randomly selected voters across all fifty states found that 54 percent favor the proposed tax reform. We can therefore conclude that a majority of voters in the country probably favor the tax reform.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Either a language acquires new loanwords through trade contact, or its vocabulary remains static. Since Mandarin has acquired many loanwords, it must have undergone extensive trade contact.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The four law review articles I read this semester all argued against expanding judicial review. It is therefore safe to conclude that most legal scholars oppose expanding judicial review.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In countries where literacy rates rose sharply, economic growth followed within a decade. Therefore, increasing literacy rates must cause economic growth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every language I have studied has irregular verbs, so there are probably some irregular verbs in every human language.

explanations.correct: The stimulus draws a sweeping universal conclusion about 'most' successful tech entrepreneurs based on a sample of three self-selected interviewees — a classic hasty generalization from a small, likely biased sample. Choice C replicates this exactly: from four law review articles (a tiny, non-representative sample), the arguer concludes that 'most legal scholars' hold a particular view. Same flaw, same structure, same probability language ('most'), same non-representative sampling problem.
explanations.A: This is a valid inductive inference. A large, randomly selected sample of 10,000 voters across all states is methodologically sound; concluding a majority probably favor the reform is a legitimate probabilistic generalization. This is a 'valid analog' trap — it superficially resembles the stimulus's move (sample → general conclusion) but commits no flaw.
explanations.B: This commits a false dichotomy — the premise presents only two options for how a language acquires loanwords, then eliminates one to assert the other. This is a different flaw category entirely, unrelated to sampling or generalization.
explanations.C: Correct. Four articles, unrepresentative sample, sweeping conclusion about 'most' scholars — hasty generalization matching the stimulus's flaw precisely.
explanations.D: This is a correlation-to-causation flaw: observing that literacy rises preceded economic growth and concluding causation. Different flaw family from hasty generalization.
explanations.E: Tempting trap — also a generalization from a personal sample ('languages I have studied') to a universal conclusion ('every human language'). However, the conclusion is 'probably some irregular verbs in every language,' which is structurally an overgeneralization. The key difference is that E's conclusion uses 'every' (a universal quantifier) rather than 'most' (a majority quantifier), and the sample in E could plausibly be a diverse linguistic cross-section, making the flaw slightly different in character. C more precisely mirrors the stimulus: small named sample → 'most' members of a professional class hold a view.
